resources.string: ActuA11y demonstrates accessibility patterns in readable source code. Each topic has two versions, switched with the toggle in the app bar: a Naive version built without accessibility in mind, and a Better version built with it. Naive versions are deliberately flawed — if one feels broken, that is the point, not a bug in this app.\n\nIf you use TalkBack, switch access, or a keyboard, try both versions of a topic and compare.
Learn how to use TalkBack (opens Android\'s official documentation)
Images and icon buttons need descriptions so TalkBack can read them aloud.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the examples below. Note what — if anything — is announced for each one, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
A smartphone icon representing a mobile device

For meaningful images, pass a non-null string to the Image contentDescription parameter — TalkBack reads it when the image is focused. For decorative images, pass null; Compose removes the node from the accessibility tree entirely.

For icon-only buttons, set contentDescription on the Icon inside IconButton. This is the only name TalkBack has for that button.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

Neither the meaningful image nor the icon button carries a contentDescription. Compose's Image only adds a semantics node when contentDescription is non-null, so the meaningful image here carries none at all — TalkBack has nothing to focus and skips it silently, indistinguishable from a genuinely decorative image. The IconButton is still a real clickable node, so TalkBack does focus it, but with no name for what it does.

The decorative image is unchanged from the Better version — a decorative image is correctly null in both, so there is nothing to contrast on that element specifically.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties

TalkBack normally reads elements in roughly the order they appear on screen, top to bottom. But when elements overlap — a button floating over the corner of a list, for example — that raw ordering can get confusing, jumping between areas in a way that does not match what the screen looks like.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the list and the round button over its corner below. Note the order things are announced in — does it finish the list before reaching the button, or does the button interrupt partway through? Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The list above carries Modifier.semantics { isTraversalGroup = true }. TalkBack's swipe order is computed by sorting the accessibility tree geometrically, banding nodes into rows by screen position. Where a floating element's bounds overlap another region — as the button here overlaps the list's last row — that geometric sort can interleave the two unless one of them is marked as an atomic group. isTraversalGroup tells the sort to treat this list as a single unit: its own children are still ordered normally within it, but from the outside it behaves as one node relative to the button.

older articles and answers describe this same idea under the name isContainer. That API still compiles today — it is only @Deprecated, not removed — but it is a dead stub: Compose's traversal sort reads only SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup and never looks at IsContainer, so code still using isContainer has no effect on TalkBack ordering even though it builds without error.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

This list carries no isTraversalGroup, so its rows and the overlapping button are sorted together in a single geometric pass, the same pass used for any sibling whose bounds intersect it.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device whether TalkBack actually interleaves the button between list rows in swipe order for this exact layout, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

Within a group, TalkBack normally reads elements left to right, top to bottom. Sometimes the visual order and the sensible reading order disagree — a dismiss button placed in the top-left corner of a card, for example, usually should not be the first thing announced.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the card header below. Note whether the title or the dismiss button is announced first, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.
Card header with a dismiss button

Both elements in the header above carry an explicit Modifier.semantics { traversalIndex = … } — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — so the title sorts first regardless of the button sitting to its left on screen.

Crucially, the Row itself also carries isTraversalGroup = true. traversalIndex only reorders siblings within their nearest enclosing traversal group; without one, it has no effect at all. See the Naive version of this same screen, which sets the identical indices but omits the group.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.TraversalIndex

This header sets the exact same traversalIndex values as the Better version — 0f on the title, 1f on the dismiss button — but the enclosing Row is not marked isTraversalGroup. Per Compose's own documentation, traversalIndex only takes effect within an enclosing traversal group; without one it is silently ignored, and TalkBack falls back to raw left-to-right order, announcing the dismiss button before the title. Nothing here looks wrong when reading the code — the indices are set correctly — which is exactly what makes this mistake easy to miss.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that the dismiss button is announced before the title here, and that the Better version announces the title first, recording the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.IsTraversalGroup

TalkBack users can jump directly between section headings on a screen, skipping everything in between — similar to how a sighted reader\'s eye jumps straight to bold section titles when skimming a page. That only works if a heading is actually marked as one; text that merely looks bold, with no underlying semantics, is invisible to that navigation mode.

Turn on TalkBack, switch its reading control to \"Headings\", and try jumping between the three section titles below. Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare — the text looks identical in both, but only one version can actually be jumped between.
Manage your sign-in details and linked accounts.
Choose which alerts you receive and how.
Control what data is shared and with whom.

Each section title above carries Modifier.semantics { heading() }, in addition to its bold titleMedium styling. TalkBack\'s \"Headings\" reading control uses exactly this property — not text size or font weight — to decide what counts as a heading, so a user in that mode can swipe directly between \"Account\", \"Notifications\", and \"Privacy\", skipping the body text under each.\n\nSee: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

These section titles are styled identically to the Better version — same font, same weight, same size — but carry no heading() semantics. Visually they read as headings; to TalkBack's "Headings" navigation they do not exist at all, so a user in that mode finds nothing to jump between and has to fall back to swiping through every line of body text to find a section.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Heading

A pane is a visually distinct portion of a screen — a tab\'s content area, the inside of an open drawer — that can change without a full screen navigation. TalkBack has no built-in way to notice a pane\'s content changed unless the app tells it, the same way it is told the screen\'s own name when a topic first opens.

Turn on TalkBack and switch between the two view options below. Note whether anything is announced when the content underneath changes, then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

Processed: 128

The content pane below carries Modifier.semantics { paneTitle = … }, and that string changes to match whichever view is selected. Per Compose's own documentation, a pane is a visually distinct portion of a window whose appearance or content can change independently — accessibility services can only announce that a pane changed if the pane's title itself changes when its content does. Switching between Summary and Details here never navigates anywhere; the same composable stays on screen throughout.

Contrast this with the paneTitle already set on this screen's own root — that one announces the screen's name once, on arrival, like every topic in this app. This one is expected to fire again on every selection change, which is the distinction requirements draw between "pane titles" as its own topic and the paneTitle every screen already carries.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack announces the new pane title each time the view switches, and record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.PaneTitle

This content pane switches between the same two views as the Better version, with identical layout and text — but it carries no paneTitle of its own, only the screen-level one set once when the topic first opened. TalkBack has no signal that the content underneath changed at all: no announcement, and focus does not move, so a user relying on TalkBack may not realize anything happened after tapping Summary or Details.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.PaneTitle

When a picker or dialog closes, a sighted user\'s eyes naturally return to whatever opened it. TalkBack\'s focus does not do that on its own — once the picker\'s content disappears, focus has nowhere defined to go, and can land at the top of the screen or be lost entirely.

Turn on TalkBack, move focus to the button below, open the picker, choose a frequency, and notice where TalkBack\'s focus lands once the picker closes. Then switch versions with the toggle in the app bar and compare.

The button above carries Modifier.focusRequester(…), and a LaunchedEffect calls requestFocus() on it once the picker closes. Compose does not hand focus back to whatever opened a dialog on its own; without an explicit request, where focus goes next is undefined.

Getting that call to actually succeed took two extra steps not obvious from the API alone — confirmed by an instrumented test on a real device (Pixel 9 Pro, API 37, Compose BOM 2025.05.00), not merely reasoned about: (1) waiting for LocalWindowInfo.current.isWindowFocused, since the dialog is a separate platform Window and hands focus back to the Activity asynchronously; and (2), the less expected one, calling InputModeManager.requestInputMode(InputMode.Keyboard) first. A Button's click target uses Focusability.SystemDefined internally, which refuses requestFocus() outright whenever the platform's current input mode is Touch — the default on any touchscreen device, unaffected by whether TalkBack is running, since TalkBack's own swipe gestures are still touch events. Skip that call and requestFocus() silently returns false with no exception, every time, regardless of the window-focus wait.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device that TalkBack's own accessibility-focus cursor actually follows this button back after the picker closes — Compose's Focused state and TalkBack's cursor are related but distinct, and only the former is what this developer note and its instrumented test can confirm without TalkBack running. Record the Compose BOM version and API level tested.

See: androidx.compose.ui.focus.FocusRequester, androidx.compose.ui.focus.Focusability, androidx.compose.ui.input.InputModeManager

This picker opens and closes exactly like the Better version — same dialog, same options, same button — but the button never requests focus back afterwards. Once the picker's content leaves the tree, nothing tells Compose's focus system where to go next, so the outcome is undefined by this code; a TalkBack user has no guarantee of returning to where they were and may need to re-explore the screen from scratch.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.focus.FocusRequester

Some apps show a short numeric code — a PIN — as a row of boxes rather than a plain text field, with a button to reveal or hide what you\'ve typed. Getting that right for someone using a screen reader is trickier than it looks.

Turn on TalkBack. Enter a PIN below, then use the show/hide control. Listen for what — if anything — is announced when you toggle it, and check what actions TalkBack offers when you explore the field itself.

The naive version renders the PIN as six separate text fields and swaps each box's literal displayed text between the digit and a bullet character to fake masking. This version instead binds one BasicSecureTextField (androidx.compose.foundation.text, stable since Compose Foundation 1.8) to a single TextFieldState, decorated to draw the same six-box appearance around it. TalkBack now has exactly one field to explain and edit, not six — and only one set of text-editing actions, not six repeated copies of it.

BasicSecureTextField unconditionally marks its semantics node isPassword = true and sets contentType = ContentType.Password — confirmed by reading BasicSecureTextField.kt directly, not assumed from its name. isPassword is the same marker Android's accessibility API exposes as AccessibilityNodeInfo.isPassword, and contentType is what lets a password manager's autofill offer to fill this field at all — neither happens automatically on a hand-built field of plain text boxes, regardless of how it looks.

The show/hide control is a Modifier.toggleable(role = Role.Switch) with an explicit stateDescription ("PIN hidden" / "PIN visible"), not a button whose own label swaps between "Show" and "Hide". That is deliberate: state belongs on the control that owns it, announced the way TalkBack expects a two-state control to announce itself, rather than depending on whatever event the field happens to fire when its displayed value changes underneath it.

That said, this is not a fully solved problem. Confirmed by reading Compose's own event-dispatch code (AndroidComposeViewAccessibilityDelegateCompat.android.kt): Compose only suppresses the text-change announcement automatically when a field's isPassword flag itself flips between true and false (bug b/247891690). This field's isPassword stays true throughout — only its TextObfuscationMode changes — so that particular guard does not apply here, and toggling reveal may still surface a text-change event carrying the real value. TODO(verify): confirm on a real device — record TalkBack version, vendor, and whether the system's "speak passwords" setting is on — whether toggling reveal here is audibly silent, masked, or leaks the PIN through the change event regardless of the isPassword marker. The source only tells us what event Compose dispatches, not what TalkBack does with it.

The field still exposes standard text-editing actions (move cursor, select text) inherited from being a real editable field. Whether those make sense on a fixed-length numeric code is a separate, still-open question.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.text.BasicSecureTextField, androidx.compose.foundation.text.input.TextObfuscationMode, androidx.compose.ui.autofill.ContentType, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.Password

Each digit lives in its own text field — six separate focusable, editable elements for what is conceptually one six-digit value. TalkBack has to be swiped through all six individually just to reach or review the PIN, and each one exposes a full text-editing action set (select all, move cursor, cut, copy, paste) that makes little sense for a single character.

None of the six carries Password semantics. Masking here is done by hand: each box's actual displayed text is swapped between the digit and a bullet character, rather than using the framework's own password mechanism (isPassword, which the classic TextField derives automatically from PasswordVisualTransformation — confirmed by reading CoreTextField.kt). Because these fields never carry that marker, TalkBack has no signal this is sensitive content at all, and a password manager's autofill has nothing to attach to either.

The show/hide control's own label swaps between "Show PIN" and "Hide PIN" to communicate state, rather than using a control TalkBack recognises as a two-state toggle. And because each box's displayed text is what actually changes when you toggle it — real digits replacing bullet characters, or the reverse — toggling reveal fires an ordinary text-changed accessibility event carrying the real value as its before/after text, once per box, since none of these fields carry the isPassword marker that lets Compose recognise and suppress that event (see the Better version's developer note).

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device what TalkBack actually announces for that event on a plain, non-password field — this is the concrete shape of the "bullet bullet bullet replaced with 1 2 3" bug this topic is modelled on.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.text.BasicSecureTextField

A plain vertical list — no grid, no table, just one column of items — has a position and a total that a screen reader can announce, like \"item 8 of 24\". Whether that announcement actually happens is not automatic, even though it looks like it should be.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the list below. Listen for whether TalkBack tells you your position in the list — \"item 3 of 24\" — or says nothing about position at all.

Both versions render this list with a plain LazyColumn — and LazyColumn already attaches CollectionInfo semantics to itself automatically, with no code from either version asking for it. That sounds like this topic should build itself. It doesn't: reading LazyLayoutSemanticState.kt directly shows the value it supplies is CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1) unconditionally — always "unknown", regardless of how many items are actually in the list, static or not. There are 24 fixed, fully-known items here, and LazyColumn's own default still reports the total as unknown.

This version overrides that default explicitly: Modifier.semantics { collectionInfo = CollectionInfo(rowCount = items.size, columnCount = 1) } layered onto the same LazyColumn. Confirmed by an instrumented test on a real device (Pixel 9 Pro, API 37, Compose BOM 2025.05.00), not just assumed from reading the API: this override is not merely plausible, it actually wins — the fetched semantics node reports the real count, not LazyColumn's internal -1. (The equivalent question for LazyVerticalGrid — where the internal default is arguably more actively misleading rather than just unhelpfully conservative — is still an open question in this project; see requirements §3.2.1 / Topic 7.)

Each item also carries its own CollectionItemInfo(rowIndex = index, …). This is never auto-supplied by any Lazy layout — confirmed by searching Compose Foundation's own source for every place it sets collectionItemInfo, which is nowhere. A collection container reporting a correct count does nothing for "item 8 of 24" without each item independently reporting which position it is.

TODO(verify): confirm the exact TalkBack announcement wording on a real device with TalkBack running — the source and the instrumented test confirm what semantics Compose exposes, not what TalkBack says out loud.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyLayoutSemanticState, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionItemInfo

This list uses a plain LazyColumn with no accessibility code added at all — which might reasonably be assumed to mean TalkBack gets no positional information whatsoever. That is not quite what happens. LazyColumn attaches its own CollectionInfo semantics automatically (confirmed by reading LazyLayoutSemanticState.kt), so TalkBack does receive something — it is just always CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1), meaning "unknown", no matter how many items the list actually holds. These 24 items are fixed at composition; the real count is never in doubt. The default here is not a gap so much as a permanent, confident "I don't know" that a developer who never checked would have no reason to suspect.

Each item also carries no CollectionItemInfo of its own — nothing in Compose supplies that automatically for any Lazy layout, so "item 8 of 24" cannot be announced here even in principle, regardless of what the container reports.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyLayoutSemanticState

Some grids are genuinely two-dimensional — a column is not just a visual lane, it is a distinct field with its own meaning, like a price or a stock count next to a product name. Compose has no table composable at all; a table like this is built by hand out of ordinary rows and cells.

Turn on TalkBack and move through the table below, cell by cell. Listen for whether TalkBack ever relates a cell back to its row and column — does \"$9.99\" get tied to the product it belongs to, or is it just a number in a stream of unconnected text?

Compose has no table composable, so this grid is built by hand: a Column of Rows, each cell a Text. Unlike LazyColumn (see the One-Dimensional Collections topic), a plain Column supplies no CollectionInfo of its own — there is no framework default here to accidentally rely on, and nothing to override. It has to be added from scratch, on both the container and every cell.

This version adds Modifier.semantics { collectionInfo = CollectionInfo(rowCount = 6, columnCount = 3) } to the table's container, and a matching CollectionItemInfo(rowIndex, rowSpan, columnIndex, columnSpan) to every one of its 18 cells, including the header row. That per-cell information is what lets TalkBack relate a cell to the row and column it is actually in — "$9.99" means nothing on its own; "$9.99, row 2, column 2" ties it to whatever is in that row's first cell.

One honest limitation: CollectionItemInfo in this Compose version carries only position and span — rowIndex, rowSpan, columnIndex, columnSpan — with no separate flag marking a cell as a header, confirmed by reading its full constructor in SemanticsProperties.kt. The header row here is simply row 0; nothing in this API distinguishes it from a data row. TODO(verify): confirm on a real device whether TalkBack gives header-row cells any different treatment at all, since this API surface does not ask for it explicitly.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionItemInfo

This is the same six-row, three-column grid, built the same way — a Column of Rows of Text cells, since Compose has no table composable. No CollectionInfo, no CollectionItemInfo, anywhere. Unlike the One-Dimensional Collections topic, there is no framework default quietly filling in a wrong-but-present value here either: a plain Column supplies nothing on its own, so this genuinely is silence, not a confidently wrong default.

TalkBack swipes through 18 individual text nodes with no indication that any of them relate to each other. "Widget", "$9.99", and "42" are three unconnected pieces of text in a stream, not a row — there is no way to tell, from what TalkBack announces, that the second cell is that first product's price rather than some unrelated number.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.CollectionInfo

A contacts list grouped by first letter, with a pinned header for each letter that stays visible while its group scrolls past underneath it — a common real-world pattern for anything alphabetical, and one that is easy to get an accurate position count wrong for even with the best intentions.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe down through the contacts below, past several pinned letter headers. Listen for whether TalkBack ever announces your position among the contacts, and whether it can tell you moved from one letter\'s heading to the next.

This list is built from five separate stickyHeader()/items() block pairs, one per letter group — not a single items(count = N) call like the One-Dimensional Collections topic. That structural difference is the whole point of this topic: the itemContent lambda passed to items(count, …) { index -> … } does receive an index, but reading LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt shows it is computed as val localIntervalIndex = globalIndex - interval.startIndex — local to that one items() call, resetting to 0 at the start of every letter group. Wiring that straight into CollectionItemInfo.rowIndex, the way a single-items()-call list safely can, would silently repeat positions from zero in every group after the first.

This version instead precomputes each contact's position across the whole flattened list before the LazyListScope body runs, so it stays correct no matter which stickyHeader()/items() block a given contact falls into. CollectionInfo.rowCount is likewise the real contact count only — 9, not the 14 a naive count of every emitted item (5 headers plus 9 contacts) would give.

Each header carries Modifier.semantics { heading() } for TalkBack's heading-navigation, but deliberately no CollectionItemInfo: this Compose version's CollectionItemInfo has no way to flag a row as a header at all (see the Genuine Tables topic), so a section header simply is not part of the row-index space here.

One fact worth knowing precisely because it looks similar and is not: stickyHeader() does receive a correct, framework-computed global index of its own. LazyListIntervalContent.kt shows headerIndex = intervals.size, captured at registration time — confirmed via IntervalList.kt, whose size is documented as the total item count across all intervals, not the number of interval calls. It is a real, correct index; it is just answering a different question than the one this topic's row index needs.

TODO(verify): confirm on a real device with TalkBack what a pinned sticky header does to positional announcements while it stays visually fixed at the top during a swipe past the contacts underneath it — the source above establishes what Compose reports, not what TalkBack does with it while a header is pinned.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyDsl.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyListIntervalContent.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.IntervalList.kt

This is the same five-group, nine-contact list, built the same way — stickyHeader() for each letter, items() for the contacts under it — with no accessibility semantics added anywhere. LazyColumn still attaches its own CollectionInfo automatically (see the One-Dimensional Collections topic), always as CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = 1) regardless of the real count, so the container reports "unknown" rather than 9. No item, header or contact, carries any CollectionItemInfo, since no Lazy layout ever supplies that on its own.

Even a well-intentioned attempt at a fix would be easy to get wrong here without knowing one specific fact: the index parameter delivered to items(count) { index -> … } is local to that one items() call, not a position in the whole list — reading LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt confirms it is computed as the global index minus that call's own start position. This list is built from five separate stickyHeader()/items() pairs, so that index silently resets to 0 at the start of every letter group; wiring it directly into a row index, as a single-items()-call list can safely do, would produce wrong, repeating positions here rather than an honest "unknown".

The section headers also carry no heading() marking, so TalkBack's heading-navigation has no letter groups to jump between — a sighted user sees the alphabet structure at a glance; a TalkBack user gets nine contacts and five pinned labels in one undifferentiated swipe order.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.LazyDsl.kt, androidx.compose.foundation.lazy.layout.LazyLayoutIntervalContent.kt

Input that is actually a button

Date, time, colour, and location pickers are almost always styled to look like a text field, but nothing about them should look editable — tapping one never lets you type a date; it opens a picker. Two common ways of building that turn out to be wrong, in different ways.

Turn on TalkBack and move to the field below. Listen for what TalkBack offers: does it sound like something you could type into, or edit the cursor position of — or does it sound like a button that opens something?

This field is not a TextField at all — it is OutlinedTextFieldDefaults.DecorationBox, which supplies exactly the visual shell (outline, label, trailing slot) with none of the editing machinery underneath it. There is no cursor, no EditableText, no SetText action to expose, because there is no editable text core here to expose it from.

The whole shape is one clickable target carrying Role.Button, with an explicit contentDescription built as "label, value" — "Appointment date, March 14, 2026" — composed from a format string, never as the literal word "button" appended by hand: Role.Button already makes TalkBack append that itself, and writing it manually would double it, exactly the "Save button, button" problem the Content Descriptions topic documents for the same reason.

Focus return once the date picker dialog closes reuses, unchanged, the exact two-step fix established and confirmed on a real device by the Focus After Navigation topic: wait for LocalWindowInfo.current.isWindowFocused before requesting focus, and call LocalInputModeManager.current.requestInputMode(InputMode.Keyboard) first, since a touch-mode focus request on a clickable target is silently refused otherwise. See CLAUDE.md's "Compose Focus Behaviour" section for why both steps are required together.

TODO(verify): confirm the exact spoken order of label, value, and role on a real device with TalkBack running — the source above establishes what semantics Compose exposes, not the precise wording TalkBack composes from them.

See: androidx.compose.material3.OutlinedTextFieldDefaults, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.Role

This field is a real OutlinedTextField with readOnly = true — the more tempting of the two common wrong attempts, because it looks like the smallest possible change from an ordinary editable field. It still carries a real editable-text core underneath, just one whose value can't be changed by typing: TalkBack still offers cursor movement and text-selection actions that do nothing useful on a fixed value, and nothing marks this as a button rather than a field someone could type into. The field the user actually needs to interact with is a separate calendar icon button next to it — a second, disconnected stop with its own generic "Open date picker" label, not tied to the field's current value at all.

The other common wrong attempt, not built here: OutlinedTextField(enabled = false). It looks like a smaller change again, but is arguably worse — TalkBack announces the whole field as disabled, which tells the user this is not actionable, for what is meant to be the primary control on the screen. Whichever of the two a developer reaches for, both fail for the same underlying reason: the fix is not about which TextField parameter to flip, it is that this was never an editable-text control to begin with.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.material3.OutlinedTextFieldDefaults
A settings row with a label, a description, and a Switch is one control, not three — the whole row should be tappable, and TalkBack should meet it once, not as three unrelated stops.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the Wi-Fi row below. Count how many separate stops it takes to get from the label to the switch, and listen for whether the switch alone ever tells you what it controls.
Connect automatically to available networks when in range.

This row is one control: Modifier.toggleable(value = wifiEnabled, onValueChange = { … }, role = Role.Switch) on the Row itself, combined with Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {}, merges the label, the description, and the switch's toggled state into a single accessibility node. Role.Switch is set on the row — the container — not on the inner Switch: the row is the node TalkBack actually lands on as the control, so that is where the role belongs.

The half that is easy to miss even after getting the row right: the inner Switch itself is Switch(checked = wifiEnabled, onCheckedChange = null). Passing null, rather than omitting the parameter or reusing the row's own callback, is what stops the switch from independently registering its own click action — leave it non-null and TalkBack meets this control twice: once as the merged row, and again as a second, separately focusable switch with no label of its own. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading the switch's own unmerged semantics node directly: with onCheckedChange = null it carries no click action at all, only the visual ToggleableState the row's merge picks up.

One more fact worth knowing, and easy to get backwards: within one merged node, the order text is concatenated in — label, then description, then the switch's state — follows structural composition order. Reading SemanticsNode.kt's mergeConfig, which walks children in zSortedChildren (paint) order, confirms traversalIndex is never consulted during that walk at all. traversalIndex reorders which node TalkBack visits next among separate sibling nodes; it has no effect on the order properties merge into inside a node that is already merged.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsNode, androidx.compose.foundation.selection.toggleable

This is the same label, description, and Switch, laid out the same way, with no accessibility work done: no Modifier.toggleable and no mergeDescendants on the row, so nothing ties the three together into one control. TalkBack meets three disconnected stops — the label text, the description text, and the switch — exactly the "one control, not three" problem this topic is about.

The switch is the worse of the three stops: Switch(onCheckedChange = { … }) is fully interactive on its own — Compose's Switch composable carries its own Role.Switch and toggle semantics without any help from this code — so it does work when tapped, but it carries no label or description of its own. A TalkBack user who lands on it via swipe hears only "Switch, on" or "Switch, off", with nothing connecting it back to "Wi-Fi" unless they happen to remember passing that text moments earlier.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.selection.toggleable, androidx.compose.material3.Switch

A row of colour swatches with no visible text at all — picking one is meant to work like a group of radio buttons, where exactly one is selected and TalkBack can say which one, and how many there are to choose from.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe across the swatches below. Listen for three things: what colour each one is, whether it tells you which one is currently selected, and whether it tells you your position among the choices, like \"2 of 5\".

Each swatch carries Modifier.selectable(selected = …, onClick = { … }, role = Role.RadioButton) — the same selectable + Role.RadioButton pattern already used for the Focus After Navigation topic's frequency picker. That gives TalkBack a real selected/not-selected state per swatch, not just a click target.

The row itself carries Modifier.selectableGroup(), wrapping all five swatches. Without it, each selectable node is still individually correct, but TalkBack has no way to relate them to each other as one group — selectableGroup() is what makes TalkBack announce a swatch's position within the group, "2 of 5", the same way a real RadioGroup does in the View system.

Each swatch also carries its own contentDescription naming the colour — "Red", "Blue", and so on — since these are plain colour circles with no visible text at all. Selected state alone ("selected, radio button, 2 of 5") means nothing without also knowing what the thing selected actually is; a description alone means nothing without knowing whether it is the current choice. This topic needs both halves together — a real implementation that supplies only one, as the Naive version here does, is common.

Each swatch carries a contentDescription naming its colour, so TalkBack does say "Red", "Blue", and so on when landing on one — the more obvious half of what an icon-only control needs, and the one a developer reaches for first. Tapping one works too, via a plain Modifier.clickable.

What is missing is the other half: no Modifier.selectable, no Role.RadioButton, and no selectableGroup() anywhere. TalkBack has no way to say whether a given swatch is the current choice, or how many options there are, or which position this one is in among them. A sighted user sees the selected swatch's border and can tell the current state at a glance; a TalkBack user hears five identically-behaving buttons with no indication that they are mutually exclusive, or which one is currently active.

A 24dp icon is easy to read, but easy to read is not the same as easy to hit. The area that responds to a tap can be larger than what is drawn, and whether it actually is makes a real difference for anyone with limited fine motor control — not just for TalkBack users.

If you have a device with an accessibility touch-target-size setting, or simply try tapping near the edge of the icon below rather than dead centre, notice how forgiving — or not — the tappable area is.

This button is a plain IconButton, and nothing else — no explicit size, no extra modifier at all. IconButton's own default implementation applies Modifier.minimumInteractiveComponentSize() internally. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading the node's own layout bounds back: its container measures 40dp × 40dp, real reserved space that is larger than the Naive version's explicit 24dp × 24dp and cannot be encroached on by a neighbouring element.

Reading SemanticsModifierNode.kt and NodeCoordinator.kt shows Compose separately auto-expands any clickable node's touchBoundsInRoot — the pointer-hit-test region the semantics tree tracks, gated only by a click action being present, using androidx.compose.ui.platform.ViewConfiguration.minimumTouchTargetSize (48dp by default) — regardless of whether minimumInteractiveComponentSize() was ever called. A disabled button and a missing button look the same to a sighted user — both simply do nothing when tapped. To TalkBack they can be very different: one is a control that exists but is not currently available; the other, built the wrong way, is not there at all.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the Submit button below before checking the box above it, then check the box and swipe past again. Listen for whether the button is ever announced before the box is checked, and if so, what it says about its own state.

Reading Clickable.kt's AbstractClickableNode.applySemantics() shows exactly what that buys: the onClick action is registered unconditionally, before enabled is even checked; only afterwards, if enabled is false, does it call disabled(). A disabled control still has its role and its (inert) action recognised by TalkBack, on top of being marked disabled — not neither.

Confirmed by an instrumented test reading the button's own semantics node back: before the checkbox is checked, it carries Role.Button and SemanticsProperties.Disabled together. The checkbox itself reuses the same toggleable + mergeDescendants + Checkbox(onCheckedChange = null) pattern already established by the Composite Controls topic; that part is not new here.

This Do Not Disturb switch is not Android\'s built-in Switch — it is drawn from scratch with Canvas. Visually it is identical, but building a control from your own drawing means taking on responsibility for everything the platform would otherwise have handled automatically.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the switch below. Notice whether TalkBack calls it a switch, whether it says on or off, and whether it names what it controls at all.
Silence notifications until turned back on.

Same Canvas-drawn track as the Naive version, same tap-handling family — Modifier.toggleable(role = Role.Switch) replaces the bare clickable and adds exactly what a Canvas draw call cannot supply on its own: Role.Switch, a ToggleableState derived from the current value, and (via an explicit contentDescription) the label this control has no Text composable to merge with.

Compare Topic 11, Composite Controls: a real, unmodified Switch() there gets Role.Switch and ToggleableState for free from the platform, and only the label-merge step (mergeDescendants) has to be added by hand. Here, replacing the platform composable with a hand-drawn one moves all three responsibilities onto this code, not just the merge — the general rule is the layer boundary itself: a component gets exactly as much accessibility support for free as it keeps of the platform's own implementation, and none of what it replaces.

See: androidx.compose.foundation.selection.toggleable, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.Role.Switch, androidx.compose.material3.Switch (Topic 11) for the free-by-default comparison.

The switch's visual — track and thumb — is drawn entirely with Canvas, and its tap handling comes from a bare Modifier.clickable. Reading Clickable.kt's AbstractClickableNode.applySemantics() confirms clickable() always registers a real SemanticsActions.OnClick action, regardless of what was drawn — so TalkBack does stop here and does respond to a double-tap.

What it does not get, because none of it is Compose's job to invent from a Canvas draw call, is Role.Switch, a ToggleableState, or any label: there is no Text composable in this subtree for a semantics merge to pick up, and Canvas itself carries no semantics of its own. The result is a control TalkBack finds and can activate, but can say almost nothing about — arguably a worse outcome than a control that is skipped outright, since nothing in the announcement itself signals that something is missing.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.clickable, androidx.compose.foundation.selection.toggleable

A control\'s name and its current state are two different pieces of information. "Show details" is the name — it never changes. "Expanded" or "collapsed" is the state — it does. Folding both into one string is a common shortcut that reads fine on screen and loses information the moment it is spoken aloud.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto "Show details" below, then activate it and swipe back onto it again. Listen for whether TalkBack announces the same control that has changed state, or what sounds like an entirely different control.
Room 204, second floor. Parking is available in Lot C; enter from the north side of the building.

Same Row, same click handling as the Naive version — role, contentDescription, and stateDescription are set explicitly rather than folding the expanded/collapsed information into one string. contentDescription stays the fixed name ("Show details") in both states; stateDescription alone carries the part that changes. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this node's own semantics back across a click: ContentDescription is identical before and after, StateDescription differs.

This is the same separation Compose's own built-in toggle controls already make internally: Role.Switch's ToggleableState (Topic 11, Composite Controls) and Role.RadioButton's Selected (Topic 12, Selectable Icon Lists) both keep a control's name constant while a separate property carries what changed. This topic builds that same separation by hand, for a custom disclosure control with no ready-made role to reach for. The same principle applies anywhere state is easy to cram into a label instead — a loading spinner's ProgressBarRangeInfo.Indeterminate (Topic 16, Progress and Sliders) is another example, not a different rule.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.StateDescription

contentDescription is rebuilt as "$label, $state" every time expanded changes, folding the changeable half of the announcement into the same string as the control's stable name. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this node's own semantics back across a click: its ContentDescription value itself differs between the collapsed and expanded states, and it carries no StateDescription property at all — there is nothing else here for TalkBack to read separately.

The practical cost: TalkBack hears what sounds like an entirely new name for the control on toggle, not the same control changing state, because contentDescription has no notion of "this text names the control" versus "this text describes what changed" — it is one opaque string either way.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.StateDescription

Some information changes on screen without the user asking a question that triggers it — a status refreshing, a search result count, a form telling you it saved. A sighted user simply sees the new text appear. Without extra work, a TalkBack user hears nothing at all, unless they happen to swipe back onto exactly that spot afterwards.

Turn on TalkBack, swipe away from the status text below so it is no longer focused, then press "Refresh status" a few times. Listen for whether the new status is announced on its own, or only if you swipe back onto it.

The status Text carries Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }, which tells the accessibility service to announce this node's content automatically whenever it changes — without needing focus on it, and without a full navigation event. Polite queues the announcement after whatever TalkBack is currently saying finishes; the far less common LiveRegionMode.Assertive interrupts immediately instead, and is almost never the right choice for a status update like this one, since it can cut a user off mid-sentence for information that was rarely urgent enough to justify that.

Two nuances worth knowing before reaching for a live region, neither built into this demo but both real: a node leaving composition entirely (rather than having its text changed in place) announces nothing at all, since a live region only fires on a content change of a node that stays present; and identical text does not re-announce, because the underlying accessibility change-detection is a text diff — pressing "Refresh status" enough times to land on the same status twice in a row will not repeat the announcement, which can look like a bug rather than the documented behaviour it actually is.

See: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.LiveRegion, androidx.compose.ui.semantics.LiveRegionMode

This Text updates the same way visually on every refresh, but carries no liveRegion at all. TalkBack has no reason to look at a node it is not currently focused on, so a sighted user sees the status change immediately while a TalkBack user hears nothing until they manually swipe back onto it — the change is silent unless the user happens to go looking for it.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsProperties.LiveRegion

Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the upload section below, pressing "Advance" a couple of times as you go. Listen for whether TalkBack ever reports a percentage or any value for the bar itself.

Modifier.semantics { progressBarRangeInfo = ProgressBarRangeInfo(current = progressPercent, range = 0f..100f) } is what makes an accessibility service treat this as a progress indicator at all: it lets TalkBack report a value against a known range as progress changes, and an explicit contentDescription supplies the name that value is attached to, since there is no Text composable here for a semantics merge to pick up. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this node's own semantics back after two presses: ProgressBarRangeInfo.current tracks the same value the visual width is drawn from.

An indeterminate spinner — one with no known percentage, just "working" — uses the same property with ProgressBarRangeInfo.Indeterminate in place of a numeric current/range pair; one API type serves both the determinate and indeterminate case, not two separate ones.

A sighted user watches the bar fill; a TalkBack user has no way to discover this control exists, let alone what value it holds — a plain Box carries no semantics of its own, so this is not even a stop during a swipe.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.ProgressBarRangeInfo

A photo grid looks two-dimensional, but the column a photo happens to sit in usually means nothing — move the window narrower and the same photo lands in a different column. What a person actually needs to know is where a photo sits in the whole set: item 8 of 12, not row 3, column 2.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe through the photo grid below. Listen for whether each tile is announced with a row and column, or with its position in the whole set.

LazyVerticalGrid attaches CollectionInfo to itself automatically, but that default is unconditionally CollectionInfo(rowCount = -1, columnCount = -1) — both dimensions "unknown," confirmed by reading LazyGridSemanticState in LazySemantics.kt, and by an instrumented test reading this exact node back. That corrects an assumption this project's own requirements doc previously made: it expected LazyVerticalGrid to confidently assert real 2D structure by default; in this Compose version it doesn't, any more than LazyColumn confidently asserts a real row count.

Per requirements §3.2.1's normative rule, a photo grid where column position carries no meaning should be announced as a one-dimensional list, not a 2D grid. Modifier.semantics { collectionInfo = CollectionInfo(rowCount = 12, columnCount = 1) } overrides the grid's own unknown default with exactly that; each tile also carries its own CollectionItemInfo(rowIndex = index, columnIndex = 0), since no Lazy layout — grids included — ever supplies this automatically for any item. Confirmed by instrumented test that the override wins over the grid's own internal default, the same mechanism already established for LazyColumn in the One-Dimensional Collections topic.

A bottom sheet sliding up over a screen is easy to get right for a sighted, touch user and easy to get wrong for everyone else: where does focus go when it opens, is its appearance ever announced, and where does focus land again once it closes?
Turn on TalkBack, open "More options" below, and choose "Cancel". Listen for whether the sheet\'s appearance is announced, and whether focus returns to the button that opened it afterward.

One thing both versions of this topic share, and neither is allowed to be naive about, per requirements §4.6: ModalBottomSheetProperties() is used at its defaults in both. shouldDismissOnBackPress defaults to true (confirmed by reading ModalBottomSheet.android.kt), and the sheet's scrim wires onDismissRequest to itself unconditionally — not even configurable, confirmed in the same file. A naive implementation cannot accidentally remove either escape hatch here even if it wanted to; the naivety this topic demonstrates is entirely about focus and announcement, never about trapping anyone.

Two focus transitions and one announcement, all added by hand. Returning focus to the trigger button once the sheet closes reuses the exact two-step fix established in the Focus After Navigation topic — wait for LocalWindowInfo.current.isWindowFocused, then LocalInputModeManager.current.requestInputMode(InputMode.Keyboard), then requestFocus() — confirmed by instrumented test the same way that topic's was.

Requesting focus into the sheet's first action on open needs the same two-step fix, but placement matters: the LaunchedEffect that does it lives inside the sheet's own content lambda, not the outer composable keyed on showSheet. An earlier attempt at the latter crashed with "FocusRequester is not initialized" — confirmed by instrumented test failure, not assumed — because the sheet's content, including the FocusRequester's target node, had not necessarily composed yet when that outer effect ran. Placing the effect inside the content lambda guarantees it runs only after that content is committed, since LaunchedEffect always fires after the composition it belongs to.

The sheet content's own paneTitle announces its appearance, the same mechanism the Pane Titles topic uses for a content swap that is not a full navigation event.

Swipe gestures are common in messaging and email apps — swipe a message to archive or delete it, with no button on screen for either action.
Why there is no naive version here

A naive version of this topic would just be a screen with no custom actions at all — a real failure, but not an equivalent screen to compare against, since there would be nothing to demonstrate. The toggle above is disabled for this reason; this is the only implementation.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the message below. Open its actions (usually a swipe-up gesture or a dedicated TalkBack menu, depending on your setup) and listen for whether Archive and Delete are offered there, without needing to perform the swipe-to-reveal gesture at all.

Two ways exist to tell an accessibility service that something changed without a full navigation event. One is discouraged by Google; the other is not.
Why there is no naive version here

This topic contrasts View.announceForAccessibility against a live region — it is not a naive-vs-better comparison, so there is nothing to toggle. The control above is disabled for this reason; this is the only implementation.

Turn on TalkBack and press each button below in turn. Listen for whether both status changes are announced reliably, and notice that only one of them has anything for TalkBack to react to if it happens to already be speaking something else.

View.announceForAccessibility(text), reached here via LocalView.current with no AndroidView wrapper needed, dispatches a raw AccessibilityEvent directly — there is no semantics property behind it at all, confirmed by there being nothing in SemanticsProperties.kt for it to set. It is not merely discouraged by convention: the method itself is @Deprecated in the Android SDK, confirmed by the compiler's own deprecation warning at the call site (suppressed here deliberately, since using it is the point of this topic, not an oversight). Announcements made during a screen transition are well documented to be dropped, and because it is a fire-and-forget event rather than a durable property of a node, there is nothing for a user to discover afterward if they missed it — unlike a live region, which stays attached to the node and would be read if the user swiped onto it directly.

Modifier.semantics { liveRegion = LiveRegionMode.Polite }, the same mechanism established in the Live Regions topic, has none of these problems: the property is attached to a real node, survives being missed at the moment it changes, and does not compete with Google's own guidance.

This asymmetry shows up in what the instrumented test can and cannot confirm: the live region side has a real semantics property to read back; the announce side does not; confirmed by an instrumented test finding SemanticsProperties.LiveRegion on one status and not the other. Whether an announcement is actually heard, dropped, or overlaps another utterance is a TalkBack behaviour, not a Compose semantics fact.

Reference numbers, postal codes, and confirmation codes are read as quantities rather than individual characters unless marked otherwise — "AB1234" can come out as a large number rather than letters and digits.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the reference code below. Listen for whether it is read character by character or as a number.

withAnnotation(VerbatimTtsAnnotation(code)) { append(code) }, built into an AnnotatedString via buildAnnotatedString, marks just the code segment — the surrounding label text is untouched. Confirmed present in this Compose version by reading ui-text's TtsAnnotation.kt (VerbatimTtsAnnotation(val verbatim: String)) and AnnotatedString.kt's Builder.withAnnotation(TtsAnnotation, block) overload directly. An instrumented test reads this back via AnnotatedString.getTtsAnnotations(start, end), also confirmed present in the same file, rather than assuming the annotation survived into the rendered semantics text.

This does not close the whole gap named in requirements §3.4.1: the View system's TtsSpan additionally has TYPE_TELEPHONE, TYPE_DIGITS, TYPE_MONEY, and TYPE_ORDINAL, each telling the TTS engine a different way to read a value; Compose exposes only VerbatimTtsAnnotation, a single "read this literally" marker. Phone numbers in particular have no clean Compose answer — a phone number read digit-by-digit is not the same as one read the way a phone TTS engine would normally group it. Topic 36 (View interop, not yet built) is the escape hatch for cases needing full TtsSpan control, not something this topic can offer on its own.

See: androidx.compose.ui.text.VerbatimTtsAnnotation, androidx.compose.ui.text.AnnotatedString.getTtsAnnotations

A plain string, built with simple concatenation and no TTS annotation of any kind. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this node\'s own semantics text back: AnnotatedString.getTtsAnnotations() returns nothing at all for it. TalkBack is free to read a run of digits like this as a quantity, and a mixed alphanumeric run has no guaranteed reading at all — confirmed as an absence, not a wrong value, since there was never a value to be right or wrong about.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.text.VerbatimTtsAnnotation

Why there is no naive version here

Turn on TalkBack, try selecting the delivery notes below, then swipe onto the order reference card and look for a copy action in its local context menu.
Leave the parcel with a neighbour if no one answers. Do not leave it unattended outside; a signature is required for this delivery.

SelectionContainer around the delivery notes makes that text genuinely selectable and copyable, the same mechanism as selecting text anywhere else. The catalogue names the real failure mode this API surface has: SelectionContainer can interfere with clickable children placed inside it, since long-press and drag gestures used for selection compete with click gestures for the same touch input — a button or link placed inside one without care can stop responding to taps. Nothing clickable is nested inside the SelectionContainer here, deliberately, to avoid demonstrating a bug rather than the pattern.

The order reference Card is not real selectable text — wrapping it in SelectionContainer would not help it — but it still needs a copy affordance. Modifier.semantics { copyText(label) { ... } } (confirmed present: SemanticsPropertyReceiver.copyText, SemanticsActions.CopyText in SemanticsProperties.kt) gives an accessibility service a copy action to offer without needing real text selection underneath it. Confirmed by an instrumented test invoking this action directly, the same way an accessibility service would, and checking the resulting status text updates.

An unrelated finding while building this: the older ClipboardManager/LocalClipboardManager API is itself @Deprecated in this Compose version in favour of the suspend-based Clipboard/LocalClipboard, confirmed by the compiler's own deprecation warnings at both the type and the CompositionLocal. Copying now means constructing a ClipEntry(ClipData.newPlainText(label, text)) and calling the suspend setClipEntry from a coroutine scope, not a direct synchronous call — worth knowing for any future topic that needs to copy text, not just this one.

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the email field below. Listen for whether it is announced as being in error, and if so, whether the reason is included.

A real correction to this topic's original premise, found while building it: OutlinedTextField(isError = true) is not semantically silent by default. Reading TextFieldImpl.kt directly shows it applies its own internal defaultErrorSemantics(isError, defaultErrorMessage) modifier, which is literally `if (isError) semantics { error(defaultErrorMessage) } else this` — a real SemanticsProperties.Error is already attached whenever isError is true, with no app code required. Confirmed on-device: the automatic message is Material3's own generic, locale-dependent string ("Invalid input", read back on a German-locale device as "Ungültige Eingabe") — present, but useless for telling a user what is actually wrong.

Modifier.semantics { error(message) }, applied explicitly here, overrides that generic default with the specific reason ("Enter a valid email address") — confirmed by an instrumented test reading this exact field back: SemanticsProperties.Error carries the deliberately-authored message, not Material3's generic one. The real lesson is not "add error semantics where there were none" — it is "an automatically-supplied generic message is not the same as a helpful one," a subtler and more easily missed gap than outright silence.

This topic is deliberately narrow: it covers only the marker's content, on a field that starts already invalid. Moving focus to the first invalid field after a failed form submission is a related but separate lesson — see the Validation and Error Focus topic for that.

See: androidx.compose.material3.internal.TextFieldImpl (defaultErrorSemantics), androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsPropertyReceiver.error

isError = true is often assumed to be purely a visual switch, changing only the field's colours — it is not. Reading TextFieldImpl.kt shows OutlinedTextField applies its own semantics { error(...) } automatically whenever isError is true, using a generic, locale-dependent default message ("Invalid input") supplied by Material3 itself, not by this app. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this field's own semantics back: SemanticsProperties.Error is present, genuinely, but its value is Material3's own generic string, not the specific reason shown in the red Text below — which remains an ordinary Text with no semantic connection to the field at all.

The naive failure here is not silence — it is false confidence: a developer who never considered accessibility for this field still ships something that gets announced as an error, and could easily assume that is good enough without checking what it actually says.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.semantics.SemanticsPropertyReceiver.error

Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the field below, which already has "Alex" typed into it. Listen for whether it says what the field is for, or just reads the value back with no name.

label, not placeholder. Modifier.semantics { contentType = ContentType.Username } and ContentType.NewPassword (confirmed present: androidx.compose.ui.autofill.ContentType, SemanticsProperties.ContentType, SemanticsPropertyReceiver.contentType in the resolved ui-android sources) declare what each field is for, so a password manager can detect and offer to fill it. Confirmed by an instrumented test reading each field's own semantics back.

Worth being explicit about, since it is easy to assume otherwise: this is opt-in work on any field type, not something a plain TextField gets for free either. A password manager has no declared hint to detect or fill either field with, silently forcing exactly the users who benefit most from autofill onto the slowest, most error-prone path: typing a username and a new password by hand, character by character.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.ui.autofill.ContentType

The keyboard\'s own action button — the one usually in the bottom corner — can promise something it does not deliver. This matters as much for keyboard and switch-access users as it does for TalkBack.

Bring up the on-screen keyboard for the name field below and press its action button, then do the same for the email field. Notice whether either one does something, or whether both simply insert a line break or sit there.

KeyboardOptions(imeAction = ImeAction.Next) plus KeyboardActions(onNext = { focusManager.moveFocus(FocusDirection.Next) }) on the name field makes the keyboard's own action button actually advance to the email field; ImeAction.Done plus KeyboardActions(onDone = { ... }) on the email field hides the keyboard and marks the form ready, rather than leaving the button to do nothing.

KeyboardOptions.imeAction is genuinely wired into the semantics tree, confirmed by reading CoreTextFieldSemanticsModifier.kt directly: it calls onImeAction(imeOptions.imeAction) { ... }, setting both SemanticsProperties.ImeAction and the action that runs it. (An earlier check of this looked only in BasicTextField.kt itself, found nothing, and wrongly concluded there was no wiring at all — the actual wiring lives in a different internal file entirely.) Confirmed by an instrumented test reading each field's ImeAction back directly, and separately by performImeAction(), which simulates pressing the keyboard's own action button end to end and runs the real KeyboardActions callback, not just checks a property.

This topic is as much about keyboard and switch-access users as it is about TalkBack — an IME action that does nothing wastes a keystroke for anyone typing, not only someone using a screen reader.

A keyboard, or a switch device driving keyboard-style navigation, moves focus from one control to the next with no visible cursor of its own. Whether the user can see where they are depends entirely on whether the app draws something.
Connect an external keyboard (or a mouse and Tab key on a desktop-class device) and press Tab to move between the chips below. Notice whether you can tell which one is focused at any point.

The same pattern already established in NaiveToggle.kt, this project's own app-bar toggle: Modifier.onFocusChanged { isFocused = it.isFocused } observes the focus state of whatever focusable target sits below it in the chain — Modifier.clickable's own internal one here, no separate Modifier.focusable needed — and a border is drawn conditionally while focused. ≥3:1 contrast against the surrounding container in both themes (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.11/2.4.13) is why MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary is the colour used, the same reasoning NaiveToggle.kt's own comment gives for its choice.

An instrumented test can only confirm so much here, stated rather than glossed over: whether a ring is actually drawn is a pixel-level, sighted fact, entirely outside the semantics tree. What the test can and does confirm is that the chip is genuinely focusable and that requesting focus actually sets it — the same is also true of the Naive version, since Modifier.clickable is focusable either way. The naive/better difference in this specific topic is visual only; verifying it needs eyes on a real external keyboard, not a semantics assertion.

See: `ui/components/NaiveToggle.kt` for the original reference implementation of this pattern

Modifier.clickable makes this chip focusable — confirmed by the same instrumented test as the Better version, which finds it every bit as focusable — but draws no visible indicator of its own when focus moves to it via keyboard. A sighted mouse-and-keyboard or switch-access user tabbing through this row has no way to tell which chip, if any, currently has focus.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: `ui/components/NaiveToggle.kt`

Every function needs to be reachable without touch — not just visible, and not just reachable by TalkBack\'s own swipe gesture, but reachable by an external keyboard\'s Tab key and by switch-access scanning too.
Connect an external keyboard and press Tab repeatedly through the toolbar below. Count how many of the three actions you can actually reach.

All three actions use Modifier.clickable, including Bookmark, which the Naive version builds with a bare pointerInput gesture detector instead. clickable registers a real click action and a real focus target — confirmed by an instrumented test reading this node\'s own semantics back: both SemanticsActions.OnClick and SemanticsActions.RequestFocus are present. Every action therefore participates in the same reachability paths at once: keyboard Tab order, switch-access scanning, and TalkBack\'s own swipe traversal, since all three read from the same semantics tree rather than needing separate handling.\n\nSee: androidx.compose.foundation.clickable

Share and More use Modifier.clickable, same as the Better version; Bookmark is built with a bare Modifier.pointerInput(Unit) { detectTapGestures { ... } } instead — still responsive to a touch tap, but confirmed by an instrumented test to carry neither a click action nor a focus target at all: SemanticsActions.OnClick and SemanticsActions.RequestFocus are both absent, not merely different. pointerInput handles raw touch and gesture events directly; it has no connection to the semantics tree unless something else adds one. A keyboard, a switch-access scanner, and TalkBack\'s own linear swipe navigation — three different reachability mechanisms — all fail on this one action for the same underlying reason.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.clickable

Many people set a larger system font size than the default, some far larger than 100%%. A screen that was only ever tested at 100%% can end up clipping or hiding text once that setting changes, even though nothing else about the screen changed.
In system settings, increase the font size to its largest step (or largest together with the separate "display size" control), then come back and compare the delivery notice card in each version.
Your package was held at the local depot because the access code on file did not match. Please update the code in your account settings or contact support to arrange redelivery.

The card has no height cap and the text uses MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium's own sp-based size, so at a larger system font scale both the text and the card around it simply grow together — there is nothing to clip. The text also does not hardcode a FontWeight, so the system's separate Bold Text setting (Configuration.fontWeightAdjustment, requirements §3.6.1) is free to apply on top of whatever weight the typography style already specifies, instead of being silently overridden.

Confirmed by an instrumented test that renders both versions side by side at 3x font scale and reads each card's own measured height back from the semantics tree: the Better card's height grows past the Naive card's fixed cap.

See: androidx.compose.material3.Typography, androidx.compose.ui.unit.Density

This card is wrapped in Modifier.heightIn(max = 64.dp) and its text hardcodes fontSize = 14.sp and fontWeight = FontWeight.Normal directly, bypassing MaterialTheme.typography altogether. The height cap is in dp, which does not scale with the system font size setting at all — so once the sp-sized text grows enough to need more room than 64dp, Modifier.clipToBounds() makes the overflow actually disappear rather than merely overlapping the next element. Hardcoding FontWeight.Normal also means the system's Bold Text setting has no text weight left for it to adjust.

This is a deliberate, documented exception to this project's own rule that no screen may clip at 200%% font scale (see CLAUDE.md, Previews) — the clipping here is the entire point of the topic, not an oversight to fix.

Confirmed by an instrumented test that renders both versions side by side at 3x font scale and reads each card's own measured height back from the semantics tree: this card's height never exceeds its fixed cap.

See the Better version for the fix: androidx.compose.foundation.layout.heightIn

Status is often shown with colour alone — a red dot, a green dot — which fails two different people for two different reasons: someone with colour vision deficiency may not be able to tell the colours apart, and anyone may struggle if the colour itself is too close to the background to see clearly.
Compare the three order rows below in each version. If you have a colour-vision simulation tool, or simply squint, check whether you can still tell the three statuses apart.

Each row pairs its status colour with an Icon (CheckCircle / Info / Close) and a visible text label, so the status reads the same whether or not colour is perceptible at all. The colours themselves are also more contrasted against the card background than the Naive version's: calculated with the WCAG relative-luminance formula against the same fixed #F5F5F5 card background, delivered ≈4.70:1, pending ≈5.62:1, cancelled ≈5.16:1 — all above the 4.5:1 text-contrast minimum, comfortably above the 3:1 WCAG 1.4.11 minimum for non-text UI components.

Confirmed by an instrumented test reading this row's own merged semantics text back: it contains both the order id and the status word.

WCAG AA contrast-ratio compliance itself is a Level 2 (Accessibility Test Framework) concern per TESTING.md — its "low text contrast" check can catch this automatically — rather than something a Level 1 semantics-tree instrumented test (as used throughout this project) can verify, since the semantics tree a test like this one reads carries colour values but no notion of perceptual contrast at all; the instrumented test here only confirms the non-colour cue is present.

See: androidx.compose.material.icons.Icons, androidx.compose.material3.Icon

Some people turn system animations down or off entirely because motion on screen can trigger discomfort, nausea, or a vestibular reaction — not as a matter of taste, but as an access need. An app that always animates at a fixed speed ignores that setting completely.
In Developer Options, set "Animator duration scale" (also affects Window/Transition scale) to "Animation off", then come back and toggle the disclosure below in each version.
Estimated delivery: 3–5 business days via standard shipping. Tracking information will be emailed once your order ships.

The expand/collapse animation's duration is scaled by Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE, read once via Settings.Global.getFloat(context.contentResolver, Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE, 1f) and applied the same way the platform's own View animators already apply it: as a multiplier, not a binary on/off switch — 0 collapses the duration to 0 (instant), 1 leaves it unchanged, 2 doubles it, matching Developer Options' "Extra slow animations" setting. Compose animations do not read this setting automatically; doing so is opt-in work, confirmed by Naive's file showing the identical animation with no such read at all.

This is a deliberate, one-time read via remember, not a live Settings.Global.ContentObserver — a user who changes the setting while this screen is already open would need to reopen it to see the new duration take effect. A production app that needs to react to the setting changing while already visible would need to register an observer instead; that is out of scope for this demonstration.

Confirmed by an instrumented test of the pure scaling function itself: scale 0 yields duration 0, scale 1 leaves the base duration unchanged, scale 2 doubles it — the same function this file calls at runtime. Duration and timing have no representation in the semantics tree (the same limitation Dark Mode's colour comparison ran into, for a different property), so this is tested as a plain function rather than through a rendered node.

See: android.provider.Settings.Global, androidx.compose.animation.core.tween

The expand/collapse animation uses a fixed 400ms duration unconditionally — Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE is never read anywhere in this file. A user who has turned system animations off specifically to avoid motion-triggered discomfort still gets the full animated transition here, since nothing in this screen\'s code path is aware the setting exists.\n\nSee the Better version for the fix: android.provider.Settings.Global.ANIMATOR_DURATION_SCALE
