When the same action appears in more than one place, it should be called the same thing everywhere. A sighted user recognises the same icon at a glance. A screen reader user has only the name to go on.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the heart button next to the search result, then onto the heart button in the product details. Listen for whether the two buttons are given the same name.
Lightweight, with a reinforced toe cap. Available in sizes 38 to 47.

Both heart buttons take their contentDescription from the same string resource, consistent_identification_save_action. WCAG SC 3.2.4 (Consistent Identification, Level AA) requires components with the same function to be identified consistently across a set of screens. EN 301 549 V3.2.1 marked the matching software clause, 11.3.2.4, as void; V4.1.1 applies it to non-web software, which is why this topic sits with the WCAG 2.2 / V4.1.1 additions even though the success criterion itself is older. Nothing in Compose or Android lint can check this. Drawing each action\'s name from one resource makes drift structurally unlikely rather than a matter of two developers happening to choose the same words, and a translator translates the one string once. The instrumented test for this topic asserts that both buttons expose an identical content description.

Both heart buttons are labelled, so this is not a missing-label failure. The search result calls the action \"Save\"; the product details call it \"Add to wishlist\". Each label was presumably written by a different person at a different time, and each is fine on its own. A sighted user sees the same icon in both places and never notices. A TalkBack user hears two different names and has to guess whether they do the same thing, or try both to find out. No lint rule or automated scanner flags this, because each label is individually valid. The failure only exists between the two.

Summary cards often combine several facts into one spoken description, so that the whole card is a single stop. If those facts are strung together without breaks, they are read as one long sentence at full speaking speed, and the listener has to work out where one fact ends and the next begins.
Turn on TalkBack and swipe onto the order card below. Listen for whether you can tell where the order number ends and the delivery status begins.

The card uses clearAndSetSemantics { contentDescription = … } so that it is one TalkBack stop, and the description is built from five segments joined with a line break (\\n) instead of a space. TalkBack treats a line break inside a content description as a pause (requirements §3.9, a finding from real-world use), so each fact arrives as its own short statement. The visible card shows the same five segments on separate lines, so the spoken and visual structure match. The instrumented test for this topic asserts that the description contains exactly four line breaks. One segment here, the order number, also has a second, independent problem covered by Topic 21 (Verbatim Strings): a plain String content description cannot carry a VerbatimTtsAnnotation, so its digits may still be read as a quantity. Segmenting fixes the boundaries between facts, not how each fact is pronounced.

The card is a single TalkBack stop with a complete, accurate description; every fact is there. But the five segments are joined with plain spaces, so TalkBack reads them as one continuous utterance: \"Order 5829174 Delivered 3 items Total €42.50 Arrived on Tuesday, 15 September\". At normal speech tempo the boundaries disappear, and the order number, status and item count run into each other. No lint rule catches this: the description is non-empty and correct. The fix is small: join the segments with \\n, which TalkBack treats as a pause.
Accessibility checklists are often written for websites and then applied to apps unchanged. Some of their items do not apply to a native app at all. This screen explains one of them.
Why there is no naive version here

There is nothing to build wrongly: the requirement described below does not apply to native apps, so there is no pattern to demonstrate. The toggle above is disabled for this reason; this note is the only version.
With TalkBack on, use heading navigation to move between the three sections below.

WCAG 2.2 added success criterion 3.2.6, Consistent Help (Level A). If a set of web pages offers help, such as contact details, a contact form, a self-help page or a chat assistant, that help must appear in the same order relative to the other content on every page where it is repeated.
Why It Does Not Apply Here

The criterion is defined in terms of a set of web pages. EN 301 549, the European standard that applies WCAG to software, does not carry it over to non-web software: the corresponding software clause is void. An audit of a native Android app that lists Consistent Help as a failure has applied a web checklist unchanged.

It is still good design. If your app has a help entry point, keeping it in the same place on every screen helps everyone, and especially people with cognitive disabilities. And if your organisation also runs a website, the criterion applies there in full.

Content-only topic, with supportsNaive = false in TopicRegistry (requirements §4.5). Its registry entry sets wcagVersion = \"2.2\", since SC 3.2.6 is new in WCAG 2.2, but leaves enClause and bindingFrom null, because there is no binding software clause to cite. The point is a correction rather than a pattern: native software is assessed under EN 301 549 clause 11, not clause 9 (web), and clause 11 is not a copy of WCAG. Some success criteria are void for software, and some are worded differently. Check the clause 11 table rather than the WCAG list when auditing an app.
Accessibility checklists are often written for websites and then applied to apps unchanged. Some of their items no longer apply anywhere. This screen explains one of them.
Why there is no naive version here

There is nothing to build wrongly: the requirement described below has been withdrawn, and never had a native-app equivalent. The toggle above is disabled for this reason; this note is the only version.
With TalkBack on, use heading navigation to move between the three sections below.

Success criterion 4.1.1, Parsing (Level A), required web markup to be well-formed: complete start and end tags, correct nesting, no duplicate attributes, and unique IDs. It existed because early assistive technologies read a page\'s markup directly and could fail on malformed markup.
Why It Does Not Apply Here

WCAG 2.2 removed the criterion entirely: browsers now repair malformed markup before assistive technology ever sees it, and the problems that still matter are covered by other criteria. A native Android app has no markup for anything to parse at all. Screen readers read the accessibility tree the app exposes, not source code.

The real concern behind Parsing lives on in success criterion 4.1.2, Name, Role, Value: every control must expose what it is, what it is called, and what state it is in. Many topics in this app are about exactly that, from content descriptions to custom-drawn switches.

Content-only topic, with supportsNaive = false in TopicRegistry (requirements §4.5). Its registry entry sets wcagVersion = \"2.2\", the version that removed SC 4.1.1, and leaves enClause and bindingFrom null, because there is no binding clause left to cite. In Compose, the equivalent of \"what assistive technology reads\" is the semantics tree, exposed to accessibility services as AccessibilityNodeInfo objects. The instrumented tests throughout this project assert against that tree directly, which is the practical, native replacement for what Parsing once tried to guarantee about markup.
